title: Brighter than a galaxy
teaches: How a faint blue 'star' turned out to outshine whole galaxies, why the engine must be a giant black hole, and how one was found at the centre of our own galaxy

blocks.text: The early radio telescopes found the sky full of radio sources, which Cambridge astronomers catalogued by number. The 273rd in their third catalogue, 3C 273, was a strong one, but radio telescopes then were too blurry to say exactly where it was. In 1962 Cyril Hazard and his colleagues at the Parkes dish in Australia used a clever trick: they waited for the Moon to pass in front of it and timed exactly when the radio signal vanished and came back. That pinned it down, and at that spot there was an ordinary-looking faint blue star.

In early 1963 Maarten Schmidt at Palomar took its spectrum. It had bright lines in places no element was supposed to have them. Schmidt puzzled over them for weeks, until one afternoon he noticed that four of them were spaced in a familiar pattern: they were hydrogen's Balmer lines, the four lines of *A schoolteacher's number puzzle*, all shifted towards the red by 16 percent.

No star in our galaxy moves that fast. But a galaxy that far away, by the Hubble–Lemaître law of *Everything is running away*, would be receding at that speed, about two billion light years away. And at that distance, to look even as bright as a faint star, 3C 273 must be giving out the light of four trillion Suns: a hundred times as much as our whole galaxy. Similar objects turned up fast. They were called quasi-stellar radio sources, soon shortened to **quasars**.

It got stranger. Old photographic plates at Harvard, going back to the 1880s, showed that 3C 273 had been brightening and fading over months, and other quasars were found to change in days. That limits how big the thing making the light can be.

Suppose the source is a light-year across, and every part of it flares at once. The light from the near side reaches us first; the light from the far side arrives a year later. However sharp the flare, we see it smeared out over a year. So a source that brightens and fades within a few days can't be much more than a few light-days across: not much bigger than our Solar System.

blocks.text: A hundred galaxies' worth of light, from something the size of a solar system. Nothing known could do that.

Fusion, the Sun's engine, turns less than one percent of its fuel's mass into energy, by E = mc² (*What makes the Sun shine?*). Running a quasar on fusion would mean burning through stars faster than any galaxy could supply them. In 1964 Edwin Salpeter in America and Yakov Zel'dovich in the Soviet Union separately proposed something much more efficient: gas falling into a black hole.

Gas falling straight in would just vanish. But gas almost never falls straight; it swirls, like water round a plughole, into a flat disc spiralling slowly inwards. Rubbing against itself, the gas heats to millions of degrees and glows ferociously. By the time it crosses the horizon, it can have given out a tenth or more of its whole mass-energy as light, many times what fusion can manage. Feed a black hole of a few hundred million to a few billion Suns a few Suns' worth of gas a year, and you have a quasar.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Quasars are gas swirling into black holes of millions to billions of Suns, at the centres of distant galaxies. Their speed of flickering shows how small the engine is.

blocks.text: Quasars are distant, so we see them as they were long ago, and there are many more of them far away than near by. They were common when the universe was young, and most have gone quiet. In 1969 Donald Lynden-Bell at Cambridge drew the obvious conclusion. The black holes can't have gone anywhere. If quasars were powered by giant black holes, then the dead quasars should still be there, sleeping, in the centres of ordinary nearby galaxies, perhaps even our own.

In 1974 radio astronomers found a small, bright radio source at the exact centre of our galaxy, in Sagittarius, 26,000 light years away. It was named Sagittarius A*. Thick dust hides the centre from ordinary telescopes, but infrared light gets through, and in the 1990s two teams, one led by Reinhard Genzel using telescopes in Chile and one led by Andrea Ghez using the Keck telescopes in Hawaii, started photographing the stars around it, year after year, with cameras that correct for the blurring of the air.

The stars near Sagittarius A* turned out to be moving very fast, in tight elliptical orbits, all round the same invisible point. The best is a star called S2. It goes round once every sixteen years, on an orbit about thirty times as wide as Neptune's, and at its closest it passes within about 120 times the Earth–Sun distance of the centre at nearly 8,000 kilometres a second. From the orbit's size and period, Kepler and Newton's laws (*The falling Moon*) give the mass it is going round.

blocks.caption: S2's orbit round Sagittarius A*. The dots are where S2 was each year from 1994; the rings are where it would be if the central mass were what you choose.

blocks.text: Four million Suns, inside a space smaller than S2's closest approach, giving out hardly any light. Nothing but a black hole fits. Genzel and Ghez shared the 2020 Nobel Prize for it, with Roger Penrose, whose work comes back in *Did time have a beginning?* And S2 has done more. At its closest pass in 2018 its light came out slightly reddened as it climbed out of the black hole's pull, the slower clocks low down of *The Sun bends starlight*. And its orbit turns a little each time round, just as Mercury's does, by the amount Einstein's theory predicts.

A black hole is far too small to see from here with any ordinary telescope. Sagittarius A*'s horizon is about 25 million kilometres across, which at 26,000 light years is like a doughnut on the Moon. So astronomers built a telescope the size of the Earth: the Event Horizon Telescope, a network of radio dishes from Hawaii to the South Pole to Spain, recording on the same night, with their data combined afterwards as if they were one dish.

In 2019 they released the first image, of the black hole at the centre of the galaxy M87, 55 million light years away and six and a half billion times the mass of the Sun. In 2022 came Sagittarius A*. Both show a glowing ring round a dark centre. The ring is hot gas, its light bent round the black hole as starlight was bent round the Sun; the dark centre is the black hole's shadow, about two and a half times as wide as the horizon itself.

Nearly every big galaxy, it now seems, has a giant black hole at its heart, weighing roughly a thousandth as much as the galaxy's central bulge of stars. The black holes and their galaxies grew up together, each shaping the other, though exactly how is still being worked out.

blocks.caption: Six questions on quasars and giant black holes
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Schmidt saw hydrogen's lines in 3C 273 shifted 16 percent to the red. Why did that mean it was so bright?
choices: The shift meant it was billions of light years away, so it must be enormously bright to be seen at all
Hydrogen only shines in very bright objects
items.why: By the Hubble–Lemaître law, that redshift means about two billion light years. Something that far away and still visible must be giving out the light of a hundred galaxies.

items.ask: A source doubles in brightness in ten days. Roughly how big can it be?
items.why: Light from the far side lags behind light from the near side, smearing any change over the light-crossing time. Ten days of change means no more than about ten light-days across.

items.ask: Why can't fusion power a quasar?
choices: It turns too little of its fuel's mass into energy
items.why: Fusion gives under one percent of the fuel's mass as energy. Gas swirling into a black hole can give out ten percent or more.

items.ask: Lynden-Bell predicted in 1969 that nearby galaxies should have giant black holes at their centres. Why?
choices: Quasars were common long ago and their black holes can't have vanished
Nearby galaxies were seen to flicker
Black holes form wherever there are many stars
items.why: The quasars have mostly gone quiet, but their black holes must still be there, starved of gas.

items.ask: S2 orbits Sagittarius A* every 16 years. If the central mass were four times larger, the same-sized orbit would take…
items.why: By Kepler's and Newton's laws, for the same orbit the period goes as one over the square root of the mass. Four times the mass, half the period.

items.ask: What is the bright ring in the Event Horizon Telescope images?
choices: Hot gas whose light is bent round the black hole
The surface of the black hole
items.why: A black hole has no surface. The ring is light from hot gas, bent by gravity round the dark shadow.

summary: **3C 273 was a quasar.** In 1963 Schmidt saw hydrogen's lines redshifted 16 percent: two billion light years away, a hundred times as bright as our galaxy.
**Fast flickers mean small.** A source that changes in days is no more than a few light-days across.
**The engine is a giant black hole.** Gas swirling in heats up and gives out a tenth or more of its mass-energy as light.
**Dead quasars sleep in galaxies' centres.** Lynden-Bell, 1969.
**Our galaxy's centre: four million Suns.** S2 orbits an invisible point every 16 years; Genzel and Ghez, Nobel 2020.
**Pictures of the shadow.** The Event Horizon Telescope imaged M87's black hole in 2019 and ours in 2022.
